implementation_notes: The standard-library route builds the markup as an Element tree - Element, SubElement, ElementTree.write/tostring - which escapes text and attributes on serialization; lxml adds a full XSLT 1.0 engine (etree.XSLT(etree.parse("view.xsl"))) plus EXSLT extensions. Hand-written transformer functions returning strings are common for HTML, and the classic Transformer class is rarely worth it in Python: a module-level function per domain type is the same transformation without the ceremony.
pitfalls: ElementTree escapes text and attributes but does not validate structure: mismatched nesting or None text is only caught by the consumer, and HTML void elements need care.
Trees are mutable and not thread-safe: build one tree per request instead of sharing or mutating a module-level tree.
lxml XSLT follows libxslt semantics and does not safely process untrusted stylesheets (filesystem and network access); never load a user-supplied stylesheet.

variants.name: lxml XSLT stylesheet
variants.implementation_notes: The declarative route through lxml: parse the stylesheet once with etree.parse and wrap it in etree.XSLT, then call the compiled object per request with keyword arguments for xsl:param values and read str(result). Choose it when the model is already XML or ElementTree data and presentation is a stylesheet artifact.
variants.code_sketch:
from lxml import etree

transform = etree.XSLT(etree.parse("artist.xsl"))
result = transform(etree.parse("artist.xml"), locale=etree.XSLT.strparam("de"))
print(str(result))
pitfalls: Compiled XSLT objects are reusable but not cheap to create: cache one per stylesheet instead of reparsing per request.
lxml XSLT is XSLT 1.0 with EXSLT; code must not assume XSLT 2.0 functions.
